\chapter{Hablo, Hablas, Habla --- The Ending Says Who}
\label{ch:terminacion}
\hlchaptermodality{258}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can state why Spanish verbs change their endings, and why the pronoun can go.}

I can state why Spanish verbs change their endings, and why the pronoun can go.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablo · hablas · habla]{hablo · hablas · habla — the ending says who}

\label{lesson:ES-C66-la-terminacion-dice-quien}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{hablar} through, all six. (\emph{Hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan}.)

You have done that hundreds of times. Now here is the question nobody has asked you: \textbf{why is the ending different every time?}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: naming what you already do}]
Because the verb \textbf{agrees with its subject}. Whoever is doing the action decides the ending, every time, in every tense you have learned.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Nosotros hablamos} — the \emph{-mos} is there \textbf{because} the subject is \emph{we}.
\end{quote}

That is the rule, stated plainly for the first time, and you have obeyed it perfectly for two hundred chapters. Being able to say it matters, because an examiner can ask, and because it explains something you were told long ago without a reason.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
At the very beginning you learned you could drop the pronoun — \emph{hablo}, not \emph{yo hablo}. It was presented as a habit of the language.

It is not a habit. It is a \textbf{consequence}. The ending already carries the subject, so the pronoun would be saying a second time what the verb has already said. Spanish drops it because it is genuinely redundant.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Hablo} — the \emph{-o} IS the \emph{yo}.
\end{quote}

Which is why the pronoun comes back exactly when the ending stops being enough: \emph{habla} could be \emph{he}, \emph{she}, or \emph{usted}, so a speaker who needs to be clear says \emph{ella habla}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablo}, and name what the \emph{-o} is doing
  \item \emph{ella habla}, and say why the pronoun is needed there
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a Spanish verb agree with? (Its \textbf{subject}.)

And is dropping the pronoun a habit or a consequence? (A \textbf{consequence} — the ending already said it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
